title: Require a pre-defined model-risk kill criterion before scaling an algorithmic program with direct financial exposure
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on Zillow's shutdown of its algorithmic home-buying business. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion.

decision_statement: Before scaling an algorithmic program that commits the organisation's own capital based on a model's predictions (pricing, purchasing, underwriting), a pre-defined threshold of prediction error or cumulative loss must be set in advance, monitored continuously, and enforced as an automatic pause — not a discretionary judgement call made under pressure to keep growing the program.
decision_context: Motivated by Zillow's algorithmic home-buying program, which continued scaling through a period of model mispricing until losses had already reached hundreds of millions of dollars before the company intervened.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Algorithmic Financial Risk Board
frameworks_referenced: SR 11-7 (Federal Reserve/OCC model risk management guidance)
alternatives_considered: Monitor model performance without a pre-committed automatic pause threshold, relying on management discretion.
Set a kill criterion only for downside scenarios already experienced, rather than for prediction-error thresholds that could catch a new failure mode.

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this shutdown.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
A pre-defined kill criterion is a direct application of established model-risk-management guidance.
Compliance must be demonstrated by an observable monitoring log against the pre-defined threshold.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether a kill criterion actually exists and has been tested.
